claims.text: The patient presented to the emergency department on 05/01/26 with sudden onset severe central chest pain, rated 8/10 in intensity, described as sharp and constant, exacerbated by deep breaths and movement, with onset approximately one hour prior to arrival.
Associated symptoms included mild shortness of breath; there was no haemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, palpitations, syncope, dizziness, or focal weakness.
Past medical history includes asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis.
The patient has a known allergy to pollen.
Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent with activities of daily living, works as an IT consultant, and is a non-smoker with no alcohol or recreational drug use.
Family history was reported as nil significant.
Initial vital signs recorded at 02:10 on 05/01/26 were heart rate 110 bpm, blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, temperature 37.1°C, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air.

Initial examination on 05/01/26 revealed mild distress, mild tenderness over the sternum, palpable subcutaneous crepitus in the neck and anterior chest wall, equal air entry, no added sounds, and no accessory muscle use.
An ECG performed at 02:30 on 05/01/26 showed sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic changes.
A chest X-ray performed at 02:50 on 05/01/26 demonstrated subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum.
The diagnosis of spontaneous pneumomediastinum was made, considered likely secondary to recent coughing or straining, with no evidence of haemodynamic instability.
The patient was admitted to the Respiratory High Dependency Unit on 05/01/26.
Medication records conflict regarding the initial analgesia regimen on 05/01/26: one record lists paracetamol 1g QDS PRN, while another lists paracetamol 1g QDS and ibuprofen 400mg TDS.
On 05/01/26, the patient was advised to avoid straining, heavy lifting, and Valsalva manoeuvres.

A physiotherapy assessment on 05/01/26 at 11:00 noted patent airway, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 96% on room air, heart rate 88 bpm, and blood pressure 120/80 mmHg; mild anterior chest tenderness and subcutaneous crepitus persisted.

Physiotherapy interventions on 05/01/26 included guided diaphragmatic breathing and pursed-lip breathing, with education on reducing intrathoracic pressure; the patient was advised to practice exercises every 2 hours while awake.

On 05/01/26, observations showed heart rate 110 bpm, blood pressure 135/85 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, temperature 37.1°C, and oxygen saturation 96%; examination showed alert patient, no respiratory distress, and persistent subcutaneous emphysema.
A repeat chest X-ray was planned for the following day to assess resolution.

On 05/01/26, the patient reported mild residual chest discomfort with no worsening symptoms; observations were heart rate 88 bpm, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Examination on 05/01/26 showed the patient was comfortable with no subcutaneous emphysema on palpation and no respiratory distress.
Omeprazole 20mg once daily was started on 05/01/26 for gastrointestinal protection against ibuprofen side effects.
On 06/01/26, the patient reported mild residual chest discomfort; observations were heart rate 88 bpm, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Examination on 06/01/26 showed the patient was alert, comfortable, with no subcutaneous emphysema, clear breath sounds, no tenderness, and no respiratory distress.
Current analgesia (paracetamol 1g QDS, ibuprofen 400mg TDS) and omeprazole 20mg OD were continued on 06/01/26.
A repeat chest X-ray on 06/01/26 showed a slight reduction in pneumomediastinum compared to initial imaging.

A physiotherapy session on 06/01/26 at 12:00 noted stable circulation (HR 88, BP 130/80), normal breathing (RR 18, SpO2 97%), and persistent subcutaneous emphysema without spread; the patient demonstrated improvement in breathing control.

On 07/01/26, the patient reported no chest pain overnight and mild improvement in breathing comfort; examination showed the patient was comfortable with normal respiratory effort and no palpable subcutaneous crepitus.
Regular paracetamol and ibuprofen were stopped on 07/01/26 as the patient was pain-free.
A repeat chest X-ray was arranged for 48 hours after 07/01/26 to assess further resolution.
Patient education regarding signs of pneumomediastinum recurrence and when to seek urgent medical attention post-discharge was provided on 07/01/26.

On 08/01/26, the patient reported no pain or shortness of breath; observations were heart rate 82 bpm, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 97% on air.
Examination on 08/01/26 showed the patient was comfortable, with no subcutaneous crepitus, clear chest, no accessory muscle use, and normal heart sounds.
Discharge planning was initiated on 08/01/26, with routine outpatient follow-up in the respiratory clinic arranged.
The patient's GP was contacted on 08/01/26 to inform them of clinical progress and discharge planning.
A final chest X-ray reviewed on 09/01/26 showed complete resolution of spontaneous pneumomediastinum with no subcutaneous emphysema or abnormalities.
The patient was cleared for discharge the day after 09/01/26, with no further imaging required.
